Works Principle
WURKS PRIN-suh-pul
noun phrase (covenant theology)
The covenant-theological principle do this and live (Leviticus 18:5; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12) by which the covenant of works operated: perfect obedience as the condition of life. Distinguished from the grace principle (the free gift of life through faith in Christ) that governs the covenant of grace.

📖 Biblical Definition

The covenant-theological principle do this and live by which the covenant of works operated: perfect, personal, perpetual obedience as the condition of life and blessing. The principle is summarized in Leviticus 18:5 (Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them), cited by Paul as the principle of law-righteousness (Romans 10:5, Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them; Galatians 3:12, the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them). The works principle governed the covenant of works with Adam: perfect obedience was the condition of confirmed life; Adam's disobedience brought death (Genesis 2:17). After the Fall, no fallen sinner can meet the works principle (Romans 3:20, by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified; Galatians 2:16); the works principle now functions to expose the impossibility of self-righteousness and to drive the sinner to Christ. Crucially, the works principle is met by Christ as the second Adam: Christ alone rendered the perfect obedience that the works principle requires (His active obedience), and His obedience is imputed to His people. The substantive contrast is between the works principle (do this and live, the principle of the covenant of works, met only by Christ) and the grace principle (the free gift of life through faith in Christ, the principle of the covenant of grace). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive distinction: the works principle reveals the impossible standard of perfect obedience that condemns the sinner; Christ alone met the works principle by His perfect active obedience; the sinner is justified not by his own works (which can never meet the works principle) but by Christ's works imputed to him through faith (the grace principle).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The covenant-theological principle do this and live (Leviticus 18:5; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12): perfect obedience as the condition of life; governed the covenant of works; unmeetable by fallen sinners; met only by Christ the second Adam; distinguished from the grace principle.

WORKS PRINCIPLE, n. phr. (covenant theology) The principle do this and live: perfect, personal, perpetual obedience as the condition of life and blessing. Summarized in Leviticus 18:5 (which if a man do, he shall live in them); cited by Paul as the principle of law-righteousness (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12). Governed the covenant of works with Adam (perfect obedience the condition of confirmed life; disobedience brought death, Genesis 2:17). After the Fall, no sinner can meet it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16); it now exposes the impossibility of self-righteousness and drives the sinner to Christ. Met only by Christ the second Adam (His active obedience imputed to His people). Distinguished from the grace principle (free gift of life through faith).

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 18:5 — "Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD."

Romans 10:5 — "For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them."

Galatians 3:12 — "And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them."

Romans 3:20 — "Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The works principle (do this and live) is the standard of perfect obedience that no fallen sinner can meet; the legalist error treats the works principle as the way of salvation; the gospel reveals that Christ alone met the works principle and imputes His obedience to His people.

expand to see more

The works principle is the standard of perfect obedience that the covenant of works required and that no fallen sinner can meet. The legalist error treats the works principle as the way of salvation, supposing that the sinner can do this and live by his own obedience; this contradicts the NT's clear teaching that by the deeds of the law no flesh shall be justified (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). The works principle, after the Fall, functions to expose the impossibility of self-righteousness and to drive the sinner to Christ. The gospel reveals the resolution: Christ alone, as the second Adam, met the works principle by His perfect active obedience (He did what Adam failed to do and what we cannot do); His perfect obedience is imputed to His people; the sinner is justified not by his own works (which can never meet the works principle) but by Christ's works imputed through faith (the grace principle). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive distinction: the works principle (do this and live) condemns the sinner who cannot meet it; the grace principle (the free gift of life through faith in Christ) saves the sinner through the imputed obedience of Christ who met the works principle on his behalf. The substantive gospel is that Christ kept the covenant of works for us, that we might receive the covenant of grace freely.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Do this and live (Leviticus 18:5; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12); the principle of the covenant of works; unmeetable by fallen sinners; met only by Christ; distinguished from the grace principle.
